newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs threaten Bosnian assembly delay.
newsitem.headline: Serbs threaten Bosnian assembly delay.

text.p: Serbs baulked at signing loyalty pledges to Bosnia on Saturday and threatened to delay the inaugural sessions of the country's new inter-ethnic parliament and collective presidency.
International mediators bargained with Bosnian Serb leaders over the ceremonies, in which the presidents and deputies were to sign oaths of office symbolising Bosnian statehood.

Colm Murphy, a spokesman for International High Representative Carl Bildt, told reporters the chances were "50-50" that Serb deputies and the Serb member of the presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, would show up.
The 42-member House of Representatives and the three-man collective presidency were chosen in general elections on September 14, nine months after the signing of a peace accord.

Although mediators had won pledges from Serb parliament deputies, the main stumbling block to the ceremony appeared to be Krajisnik -- a hardline Serb nationalist who wants to avoid a public display of support for Bosnia as a unitary state.
Krajisnik said on Friday the venue and the wording of an oath had yet to be agreed, Bosnian Serb media reported.
He said Serb deputies would assemble in their government seat of Pale, a mountain village outside Sarajevo, and prepare to drive to the city if a satisfactory solution was found.
"Failing that, the session will not take place at all," he was quoted as saying by the Serb SRNA news agency.
Michael Steiner, deputy to Bildt, was meeting Krajisnik in Pale only a few hours before the session was due to open.
"Krajisnik is playing hardball," said one official in Bildt's office, who asked not to be named.
Krajisnik, citing safety concerns, has suggested the ceremony be held at Sarajevo airport or the U.S. embassy, officials said.
If Krajisnik refused to come to the city centre, Murphy said there was little that could be done to penalise him.
"There isn't much we can do. We will do the usual things like send a strong diplomatic protest."
But he said the presidency, which met for the first time on Monday, already exists legally and Saturday's proceedings were merely a "ceremonial" ratification.
"They already have the necessary legal powers," Murphy said.

If the meeting goes ahead as planned, the three presidents and parliamentary deputies should take the stage and sign a document expressing loyalty to Bosnia and support for the Dayton peace agreement signed last December.
The three members of the presidency should also deliver short speeches.

Under terms of the Dayton peace pact, the House of Representives governs a union of Serb and Moslem-Croat territories along with a 15-member upper chamber appointed by regional assemblies, the House of Peoples or Nations.
The same Serb, Moslem and Croat nationalist parties that helped plunge the former Yugoslav republic into war prevailed in the September poll.
